analysis.one_liner: Requires annual public reports on the decommissioning of offshore oil wells, platforms, and pipelines.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 3 Democratic cosponsors, got a subcommittee hearing in July 2026 but no committee vote and no floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: When offshore oil and gas wells, platforms, and pipelines reach the end of their useful life, federal rules require companies to plug wells and remove or decommission the structures. This bill would require the Interior Department to publish a yearly report showing how many decommissioning applications were required and received, how many wells, platforms, and pipelines missed their decommissioning deadlines, how many were allowed to stay in place instead of being removed, and what enforcement actions the safety bureau has taken. The aim is to make visible an area where companies have often delayed cleanup and where taxpayers can end up footing the bill when operators walk away.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, taxpayers, and the public gain a running public record of how much offshore cleanup is being delayed and how much is being allowed to stay in the ocean rather than removed. That record gives Congress and the public the information needed to push for enforcement, and could help prevent future cases where taxpayers inherit cleanup costs from abandoned wells.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Interior Secretary to publish, on the department's website, an annual report counting how many offshore wells, platforms, and pipelines missed their required decommissioning deadlines, and how many were approved to be decommissioned in place rather than removed.

The report must also describe the status of enforcement actions by the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement, including citations, civil penalties, and disqualifications from future offshore operations.

Making this information public gives coastal residents, watchdog groups, and members of Congress a factual basis to demand that operators actually plug and remove what they are legally required to plug and remove.
Offshore wells that are not properly plugged can leak oil and other pollutants into the ocean; a public record of the backlog addresses the problem from the information side.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas operators, whose delayed decommissioning and in-place approvals would be tallied publicly each year, exposing weak spots in their compliance and in federal enforcement.

drawbacks.text: The bill only requires reporting; it does not tighten any decommissioning deadline, add a bond requirement, or force a single company to plug anything sooner. Companies could remain out of compliance as long as the noncompliance is now published.
The first report is not due until two years after enactment, so the earliest useful public accounting would be well after passage.
An annual report imposes modest paperwork and publication duties on the Interior Department, which would need to compile compliance and enforcement data each year.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a low-cost transparency measure with a real but indirect benefit: it does not itself plug any wells or change any deadline, so its value depends entirely on whether public reporting later spurs enforcement or legislation. As a first step, it is cheap and modest; as a fix for the offshore cleanup backlog, it is not one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee that held a hearing in July 2026, and it has not moved to a committee vote or the Senate floor.

narrative.text: Sen. Peter Welch introduced the Plug Offshore Wells Act in the Senate in March 2026, joined by Sens. Merkley, Wyden, and Markey.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
In July 2026, the subcommittee on Public Lands, Forests, and Mining held a hearing on the bill; no further action has been recorded.

The bill's sole operative requirement is an annual Interior Department report, published online, counting missed decommissioning deadlines, wells and platforms decommissioned in place, pipelines removed or left, and the status of safety-bureau enforcement actions.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore operators, so far: with no reporting requirement in law and no recorded committee action, the status quo of limited public accounting continues.

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited three Democratic cosponsors; the bill was referred to Energy and Natural Resources, where he has sought action.

for.name: Sens. Jeff Merkley, Ron Wyden, and Ed Markey
for.what_they_did: Joined as cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Subcommittee on Public Lands, Forests, and Mining
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill in July 2026.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and all three listed cosponsors are Democrats; no Republicans have signed on, and no recorded opposition has appeared either.

industries.note: The bill does not change any company's legal duty to plug wells or remove platforms, but it would publish an annual tally of who has missed decommissioning deadlines and escaped enforcement, increasing public and congressional pressure. Companies that delayed cleanup while keeping decommissioning costs off their balance sheets are the ones exposed.

Better-publicized decommissioning backlogs could increase plugging and removal work over time, which is performed by specialized contractors. The connection is indirect and contingent on later enforcement.

analysis.trajectory: Most Senate bills never reach a committee vote, and this one has a single subcommittee hearing, three cosponsors, and no bipartisan support. A reporting-only bill could move as part of a broader package if a sponsor attaches it to something larger, but as a standalone bill it will likely die in committee at the end of this Congress.
